structure.title: 2. The Digital Pension App (incl. 2.1 Conceptual framework, 2.2 Methods)
3.1-3.3 Natural experiment, identification strategy, empirical specification
3.4 Quasi-experimental results (incl. timing and heterogeneity subsections)

observations.statement: The paper names two estimands up front: an intent-to-treat effect of making the app available, identified from a staggered rollout across two funds, and a LATE of app usage identified from a field experiment used as an instrument for registration.
observations.locator: Introduction, paragraphs on ITT and LATE; Section 2.2 Methods

observations.statement: The identifying assumption for the rollout design is stated explicitly: the timing of the invitation letter is exogenous to individual contributions conditional on controls and fund and year fixed effects, justified by the management deciding timing on administrative grounds.
observations.quote: receiving the invitation letter in a given year is exogenous to the individual voluntary contribution

observations.statement: The institutional reason for the staggered timing is documented in a footnote reporting what fund management told the authors (limited implementation resources, learning from a pilot), with the accounting relationship between the two funds also disclosed.

SUTVA is discussed by name: spillovers would require information flow across employees of different firms using different funds, argued unlikely given the funds' size; firm-specific dynamics are argued away because members are spread across hundreds of firms.

The authors acknowledge that using both funds' rollouts requires a constant treatment effect over time (citing Goodman-Bacon) and add a canonical two-group DiD restricted to pre-2018 years with the later-treated fund as the never-treated control; the common trend assumption for this variant is spelled out in a footnote.

The paper explains why the natural experiment cannot identify the effect of app usage (self-selection into registration; take-up observed only after both funds had rolled out) and why rollout timing is not used as an instrument, motivating the experiment.

The RCT randomizes non-registered participants into a control group and three reminder-letter arms; instrument exogeneity is argued from random assignment, and the LATE is explicitly described as the effect on compliers who registered because of the letter.
For the RCT, within-firm spillovers between arms are stated as an assumption, and the direction of bias from a violation (understatement of the ITT) is given.

Data are individual-level administrative records from two occupational pension funds managed by one company, covering a stated multi-year period, linked to app registration status observed at one date; the paper describes the variables available (income, contributions, wealth, buy-in potential, demographics).

Sample restrictions on age and earnings are justified by institutional benchmarks (a typical full-time minimum wage and a top income percentile), and observations with zero buy-in potential are excluded because such individuals cannot contribute; construction details are delegated to an Internet Appendix section.
To avoid compositional changes confounding the rollout comparison, estimation conditions on the set of participants present when the fund introduced the app.

For the RCT, the two sources of attrition (retirement and employer change) are named, attrition shares over the two follow-up years are reported, and a differential attrition test between arms is placed in an appendix table.
Observation counts are printed in every main regression table and in the balance table, and the estimation sample size (observations and distinct individuals) is stated in the data section.

The representativeness of the fund sample is checked against national labor-force statistics on gender, age, income and industry, with the comparison tables placed in an appendix and summarized in a footnote.
observations.locator: Section 1.3.1; footnote 20; Tables C3 and C4

observations.statement: Outcomes are a yearly indicator for making a voluntary buy-in and the log of the yearly contributed amount with one added to handle zeros; an IHS transformation is reported as an appendix robustness check.

The event is defined as the fund's first invitation letter to register on the app; event-time dummies are relative to the year before the letter, which is the omitted category, and the DiD post dummy is defined analogously.
The three reminder-letter arms are defined by verbatim text additions and by which app screenshot feature is highlighted; letter copies are placed in the Internet Appendix.
The buy-in potential, which determines eligibility and heterogeneity splits, is defined with an explicit institutional formula and a worked numerical example in the background section.

Table 1 places the static event-study and DiD estimates side by side for each of the two outcomes, with rows for year FE, controls, pre-period outcome mean and observations; notes list the full control set, the estimator per column and individual-level cluster-robust SEs.
Binary outcomes are estimated by probit with marginal effects reported, OLS for the log amount; linear probability model versions are relegated to appendix tables and footnotes.
observations.locator: Section 3.3; footnotes 37 and 39; Tables F3, F4

observations.statement: Table 3 reports the ITT and LATE columns for registration, buy-in indicator and log contributions, with a first-stage F-test p-value row, the control mean, year FE and controls rows, and clustered SEs stated in notes.

Because instrument and endogenous variable are both binary, the LATE is estimated with a three-step procedure (probit for registration, predicted values used as instrument in 2SLS), described in a footnote citing a textbook.

Standard errors are clustered at the individual level in both the rollout and RCT analyses; the text states this but gives no reasoning for the choice, even though treatment varies at the fund level in the rollout design (only two funds).
For the RCT, minimum detectable effects for registration and for contribution probability are reported from power calculations, expressed relative to pretreatment levels, in a footnote.

For the rollout design, a pre-introduction comparison of characteristics and contribution behavior across the two funds is placed in an appendix table and discussed in the text, including where balance fails (gender share).

Pre-trends are assessed by plotting event-time coefficients with confidence bands and by reporting a joint test of the pre-event coefficients in the text; fund-specific before and after plots are shown in the appendix first as a descriptive step.
A placebo treatment assigning the app introduction to the first fund one year early is reported in an appendix table and mentioned in a footnote.

The RCT balance table in the main text compares pooled treatment with control on demographics, income, wealth, buy-in potential and tenure with t-test p-values; per-arm balance goes to an appendix table.

The first stage (letter on registration) is reported as the first column of the main RCT table and an F-test p-value row appears under the LATE columns; instrument strength is referenced in the text rather than discussed with a named weak-IV threshold.
Differential attrition between arms is tested in an appendix table and summarized as a precondition before interpreting mean differences as ITT effects.
A footnote reports an appendix check that registration status observed after both rollouts is unrelated to which fund introduced the app first.

Robustness for the rollout design is handled almost entirely in footnotes pointing to appendix tables: linear probability versions, an alternative minimum-earnings cutoff, IHS outcome transformation, and the placebo timing.
observations.locator: Footnotes 35, 37, 39; Tables F3, F5, F11, F12; Figures F4, F10

observations.statement: The canonical DiD on the pre-2018 sample is presented in the main table as a complementary estimate that relaxes the constant-effect assumption of the pooled event study, and results are described as similar.

Medium-run persistence is examined with a before/after event design without year FE, with the reason (no never-treated units after the second rollout) explained in a footnote and the limitation about time-varying shocks stated in the text.

The event study is re-estimated separately for eventual registrants and never-registrants as suggestive evidence on whether registration drives the response; the authors stress this split is not causal because registration is endogenous.

Heterogeneity by gender, income and buy-in potential is summarized in one paragraph with results placed in the Internet Appendix; distance-to-retirement heterogeneity is explored three ways (linear interaction, above-median dummy, terciles) in an appendix table.
observations.locator: Section 3.4.1; Table F6; Internet Appendix F

observations.statement: In the RCT, ITT and LATE are estimated separately by letter arm and shown as a two-panel bar figure with confidence intervals; LATE heterogeneity across arms is interpreted as evidence on channels because each letter may induce different compliers.
observations.locator: Section 4.3.3; Figure 6; Figure H1; Table H4

observations.statement: A stylized life-cycle model in the Internet Appendix motivates two frictions (transaction costs and tax misperception) and is used to argue that the rollout effect alone cannot separate the channels, which justifies the experimental design.
observations.locator: Section 2.1 Conceptual framework; Internet Appendix B

observations.statement: Complier characteristics by letter arm are described using the Angrist-Pischke approach in the Internet Appendix and discussed in a dedicated mechanisms discussion paragraph; the authors caution against reading a null information effect as full tax awareness.
observations.locator: Discussion on the mechanisms; Internet Appendix H

observations.statement: The alternative that older participants offset contributions with housing withdrawals is checked by estimating the rollout effect on home-financing withdrawals in an appendix table.

Effects are interpreted relative to the pretreatment contribution rate or control mean, converted into annual currency amounts for the LATE, and benchmarked in a footnote against effect sizes from earlier information-letter studies.
Noisy or insignificant estimates are described as such rather than dismissed, and the LATE is compared with the suggestive registrant-subsample estimate.

The authors state that without household balance-sheet linkage they cannot conclude that total household saving rises, and that the medium-run analysis is suggestive because only a small subgroup is observed transitioning into retirement.
The registrant-subsample analysis is explicitly labeled non-causal, with a further caveat that late-year registrations could bias it toward understating the effect (footnote).
The LATE is framed as local to individuals who registered because of the reminder, acknowledged as unrepresentative of the general population but argued to be a policy-relevant group.
The conclusion frames the reminder letter as a low-cost scalable intervention once an app exists and discusses distributional concerns and future research questions rather than claiming generality.

Event-study figures plot marginal effects with two nested confidence bands; figure notes state the model, the omitted period, the SE clustering, the appendix table holding full estimates, and the data source and years.

Regression tables use significance stars, report SEs in parentheses, and their notes restate the estimator, sample, dependent variable, controls, clustering and data years; the balance table reports means, differences and t-test p-values.

Main-text figures include estimated age profiles, app screenshots, a rollout timeline schematic, and mechanism bar charts; appendix material is lettered by section (A through H) and referenced from the main text by table and figure number.

There is no main-text summary statistics table; sample characteristics are given in prose and footnotes, with descriptive tables and figures (age profiles, income distributions) placed in Internet Appendix C.

The introduction previews both strategies and their results in sequence, then devotes several paragraphs to positioning against four literatures (FinTech, household inertia, reminders, retirement information).

Order is institutional setting and descriptive facts, then app description and conceptual model, a short Methods subsection acting as roadmap, then quasi-experimental design and results, then the experiment with mechanisms last; there is no separate robustness section and much of the evidence lives in the Internet Appendix.

A 'Key facts' subsection documents stylized facts (replacement rates, buy-in potential, who contributes) using pre-app years only, with a separate cantonal tax-record analysis on funding sources summarized in the main text and detailed in an appendix.
Results subsections use interrogative run-in headings (for example asking who accesses the app or whether contributions are increased or shifted) to organize the analysis.
A code availability statement at the end of the text cites a Harvard Dataverse DOI for replication code; no statement is made about data availability, and no software is named in the text.

The pension data were obtained through collaboration with the fund-managing company and linked to app registration records; cantonal tax records and aggregate app navigation statistics are additional sources; no access procedure is described.

The field experiment is stated to be preregistered at the AEA RCT registry with the registration number given in the acknowledgments and in the design section; no IRB or consent statement appears, and no deviations from the plan are discussed.

Institutional facts that underpin identification (why rollout was staggered, when letters were mailed, the seasonal timing of contributions) are documented through partner communications and appendix figures cited in footnotes.

gaps: No justification given for clustering at the individual level despite fund-level treatment assignment with two funds in the rollout design.
No data availability or access-procedure statement; only replication code is cited.
No software named in the text.
No IRB or consent statement for the field experiment; preregistration deviations not discussed.
No multiple-testing adjustment discussed across the three treatment arms and multiple outcomes.

reading.note: All 40 pages of the published text read, including references (pages 37 to 40). The Internet Appendix (sections A to H) is not part of the text file and was not read; appendix contents are recorded only as cited from the main text.
